en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Thirty, Chapter on Kiṁchanda.
5. The Sambhava Jātaka “O you who have entered upon kingship,
O lord of pure conduct!”
I desire to attain greatness and to conquer this earth,
not by unrighteousness, but by righteousness.
Unrighteousness does not please me;
only righteous conduct, which is practiced by a king of pure character, is what ought to be done.
By that through which one is not blamed here,
and by which one is not blamed after passing away,
one gains renown among gods and humans.
By which we have reached you, O Brahmin.
I, who desire to accomplish both the goal and the Dhamma, O Brahmin;
"Being asked, O Brahmin, explain to me that matter and the Dhamma.
"Nothing other than Vidhura, O King," [he replied].
This deserves to be explained:
that which you wish to do, O Kṣatriya, both for the sake of the goal and in accordance with the Dharma.
“Come now, Pahita, go to Vidhura; take this nikkha of gold, and— ”
Go to Hara, O Sucīrata;
you should present this offering for the sake of instruction in purpose and Dhamma.
Bhāradvāja, having set out with his own purpose,
approached Vidhura;
Mahābrahmā saw him there.
Unequalled in his own home:
“I have been sent as a messenger by the illustrious King Koravya.”
“You ask about both the goal and the Dhamma,” thus said Yudhiṭṭhila;
you [should consider] that goal and that Dhamma.
When questioned by Vidhurakkha:
"They will block my way to the Ganges, O Brahmin; I am not able to do it."
To even fathom the great ocean—
how could he possibly do that?
I am unable to explain it to you.
When asked about the goal and the Dhamma,
my son Bhadrakāra,
my own legitimate offspring, [spoke].
"Go, O Brahmin, and having approached him, ask about that matter and the Dhamma.
Thus spoke Bhāradvāja, whose purpose was well-attained.
The doer of good deeds went to his dwelling;
there Mahābrahmā saw him seated in his own abode.
“I have been sent as a messenger by the illustrious King Koravya, with the message:
‘Ask about his welfare and his righteousness.’”
Thus spoke Yudhiṭṭhila:
"O doer of good deeds, explain that matter to me according to both the meaning and the Dhamma."
“Leaving behind my body of flesh,
I am pursuing the iguana;
I am unable to tell you [where it is].”
When asked about the goal and the Dhamma, [I replied]:
"My brother is named Sañcaya;
he is my younger brother, pure in conduct."
"Go, O Brahmin, and having approached him, ask about that matter and the Dhamma.
Thus addressed, Bhāradvāja went to his own home.
To the vicinity of Sañcaya;
there the Great Brahmā saw him sitting in his own dwelling.
“I have been sent as a messenger by the king,
the illustrious Koravya;
he asks after your welfare and your righteousness.”
Thus spoke Yudhiṭṭhila:
"Being questioned, explain that matter to me according to both its meaning and the Dhamma."
“Death swallows me constantly,
both evening and morning, O you of pure conduct;
I am unable to tell you [otherwise].”
When asked about the goal and the Dhamma, [I replied]:
"My brother is named Sambhava;
he is my younger brother of pure conduct."
“Go, O Brahmin, and having approached him, ask about that matter and the Dhamma.
“Truly wonderful, sir, is this Dhamma!”
This is not pleasing to us;
those three people— the father and his two sons—
are not wise in wisdom.
"You are not able to explain the meaning and the Dharma when asked;
how indeed could a youth know it?"
When asked about the goal and the Dhamma,
do not despise him because he is young,
without first inquiring into his origin.
Having asked, one should know the origin,
O Brahmin, as well as the meaning and the Dhamma;
just like the stainless moon.
Traveling through the element of space,
he outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with his radiance.
Thus, even though he appears young,
his existence arises through the application of wisdom;
do not despise him, thinking, "He is a youth."
Having questioned about their origin, one should know the origin,
the meaning, and the Dhamma, O Brahmin.
Just as the month of Rammaka,
O Brahmin, is among the months of summer,
so indeed is it distinct from other months.
It is beautified by wild flowers.
In this way too, even for one who is young,
there is the arising [of beauty] through the application of wisdom.
Do not despise him, thinking,
"He is young," without having inquired about his origin;
by inquiring about his origin, one may know him.
Meaning and the Dhamma, O Brahmin—
just as Himavat, O Brahmā,
is the Gandhamādana mountain.
Covered with various trees,
a dwelling place for great hosts of spirits,
and [endowed] with divine medicinal herbs.
The quarters shine and the wind blows.
Thus too, for one who is young in form,
there is the arising [of wisdom] through the application of discernment.
Do not despise him, thinking "he is young," without having inquired about his origin;
by inquiring about his origin, one would know.
The goal and the Dhamma, O Brahmin.
Just as fire, O Brahmā,
is garlanded with flames and possessed of glory;
Blazing in the forest,
he goes like a fire along the dark path;
he whose food is oblations, whose banner is smoke.
The supreme fire of divine joy blazes forth at midnight upon the mountain peak,
shining with abundant light.
Thus, even though he appears young,
his existence arises through the application of wisdom;
do not despise him, thinking, "He is a youth."
Having questioned about the origin,
one should understand the origin,
the meaning, and the Dhamma, O Brahmin.
One knows a noble steed by its speed,
and a draft ox by its burden;
one knows a cow by her milk.
And even a wise man who is merely appearing so—
thus, even for one who is young in appearance, there is the possibility [of excellence] through the application of wisdom.
Do not despise him, thinking "he is young," without having asked about his origin;
by asking about his origin, one may know it.
“Meaning and the Dhamma, O Brahmin.
Bhāradvāja, having understood his own purpose, approached Sambhava.
The Great Brahmā saw him playing outside the city.
"I have been sent as a messenger by the king," he said.
"‘He asked about the goal and the Dhamma,’ thus Yudhiṭṭhila spoke concerning the illustrious Koravya."
"Being asked, explain to me that meaning and the Dhamma regarding its origin.
"Truly, I shall explain it to you."
Just as it is for one who is skilled,
so too does the king know whether he will act or not.
“‘Today or tomorrow,’ Sucīrata,
you should say when questioned by the king;
do not let the king become discouraged.”
When the matter had arisen, Yudhiṭṭhila,
of pure conduct, being questioned by the king, should have explained it only to himself.
One should not enter upon a wrong path like one who is deluded and mindless;
one should not overstep oneself.
One should not practice what is unrighteous;
one should not cross where there is no ford,
nor should one be intent on what is harmful.
But that kshatriya king who knows how to perform these duties always prospers.
Like the moon in its bright fortnight,
he is dear to his kinsmen and shines among his friends.
With the breakup of the body,
that wise one is reborn in heaven.
Thus ends the fifth Jātaka, the Sambhava Jātaka.
